column2: ST elevation in V1–V4 with reciprocal inferior depression means proximal LAD occlusion (anterior wall and septum). RCA gives inferior, circumflex lateral/posterior changes.
Pathological Q waves (> 40 ms or > ¼ of the R wave) in contiguous leads mean an old transmural infarct; echo can confirm a regional wall-motion defect.
A reversible defect in the apex, anterior wall and septum is LAD territory. Mediastinal radiotherapy accelerates coronary disease, especially of the proximal LAD.
ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers and eplerenone cut early post-MI mortality; an ICD in the first 40 days does not (DINAMIT, IRIS). Reassess EF after 40 days.
Predictable exertional angina limiting ordinary activity slightly (e.g. walking uphill, stairs quickly) is CCS class II. Class III = one flight at normal pace.
The test needs ≥ 85% of age-predicted maximum HR (~145/min at 50); a peak of 130 is non-diagnostic. A BP rise to 155/95 on exercise is normal.
NSTEMI causes: non-occlusive plaque thrombus (commonest), spasm, progressive narrowing, inflammation and supply–demand mismatch. Microvascular dysfunction causes microvascular angina.
Crescendo then rest angina with new T inversion is NSTE-ACS; only troponin separates NSTEMI from unstable angina, so the diagnosis awaits it (treatment starts now).
A small troponin rise with fluid overload in an anuric dialysis patient is demand injury: urgent dialysis with ultrafiltration and serial troponin/ECG. Furosemide fails in anuria.
Nitrates are contraindicated within 48 h of tadalafil (24 h for sildenafil): profound hypotension. Aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulant and beta-blocker are fine.
High-sensitivity troponin I/T is the preferred MI marker: a rise/fall with one value > 99th centile plus ischaemic evidence. CK-MB and LDH are less specific.
CK-MB rises 4–8 h after infarction, peaks ~24 h and normalises by 48–72 h (useful for reinfarction). Myoglobin rises earliest but is non-specific.
The longest delay in STEMI care is the patient's delay in calling for help, longest in the elderly, women and diabetics; system delays are now short.
ST elevation resolving < 50% at 60–90 min after fibrinolysis with ongoing pain is failed reperfusion: immediate rescue PCI. Repeat lysis is ineffective.
PCI vs CABG in multivessel disease depends on anatomy (SYNTAX), diabetes, LV function and chance of complete revascularisation: a heart-team decision.
When antegrade wiring of a CTO fails, a retrograde approach through collaterals is an option. CTO-PCI relieves angina; no proven mortality benefit.
PCI to a degenerated vein graft risks distal embolisation and no-reflow, so use an embolic protection device. LIMA grafts outlast vein grafts (> 90% vs ~50% at 10 years).
Days–weeks after catheterisation: livedo, blue toes, AKI, eosinophilia and high ESR = cholesterol atheroembolism. Contrast nephropathy starts within 48–72 h without eosinophilia.
Claudication with night pain eased by dependency is PAD; ABPI < 0.9 confirms it (< 0.4 critical). Calcified vessels in diabetes can falsely raise the ABPI.
Supervised exercise to near-maximal claudication is first line (NICE CG147). His main risk is MI or stroke; add clopidogrel and a statin. Few progress to limb loss.
Distal limb ischaemia with tapering small-artery occlusions in a young smoker is Buerger disease; complete tobacco abstinence is the only effective treatment.
Varicose veins are commoner in women, but chronic venous insufficiency with oedema is slightly commoner in men. Venous ulcers affect only 1–2% of adults.
The great saphenous vein, from the medial foot to the saphenofemoral junction, is the longest vein; it is the usual CABG conduit and the commonest site of varicosities.
A medial malleolar ulcer with haemosiderin pigment, lipodermatosclerosis and oedema after DVT is venous; treat with compression once ABPI is adequate.
NICE: lifestyle advice comes first for raised CV risk; atorvastatin 20 mg is then offered at QRISK3 ≥ 10% as a shared decision, so it is the least urgent step.
Invasive coronary angiography is the reference standard and allows PCI. NICE uses CT coronary angiography first, then functional imaging if non-diagnostic.
Fibrinolysis is indicated within 12 h of STEMI onset when PCI is not possible within 120 min; it works best in the first 3 h.
Painful blue toes with livedo but palpable pulses after anticoagulation or instrumentation is cholesterol embolism; it may also cause AKI and eosinophilia.
Lipids, smoking, hypertension and high homocysteine are risk factors. Folic acid lowers homocysteine and is not a risk factor.
Typical angina with exercise ST depression but normal angiogram is cardiac syndrome X (microvascular angina), commoner in women. Prinzmetal gives ST elevation at rest.
ACS dose of enoxaparin is 1 mg/kg SC 12-hourly (once daily if CrCl < 30). 40 mg daily is prophylaxis; fondaparinux 2.5 mg is preferred if no early angiography.
Treat an angina attack with sublingual GTN; call an ambulance if pain persists 5 min after the second dose. Beta-blockers or CCBs prevent attacks.
The inferior wall is seen by II, III and aVF (usually RCA). Septal = V1–V2, anterior = V3–V4, lateral = I, aVL, V5–V6.
Posterior MI mirrors in V1–V2: tall R, ST depression and upright T; V7–V9 show ST elevation. Treat as STEMI (circumflex or RCA).
Reperfusion is indicated for ischaemic pain with ST elevation in 2 contiguous leads, new LBBB or true posterior MI. ST depression alone is not an indication.
Septal, free-wall and papillary rupture are early complications (2–7 days). Dressler syndrome, LV aneurysm, mural thrombus and heart failure come weeks later.
Circumflex occlusion gives lateral ST elevation (I, aVL, V5–V6), often with posterior changes, and is the infarct most often 'silent' on the ECG.
At 20 min the earliest diagnostic sign is ST elevation (after hyperacute T waves). Troponin may still be normal and Q waves take hours.
With true aspirin allergy, use clopidogrel (a P2Y12 inhibitor) as the antiplatelet, plus anticoagulation and reperfusion. Warfarin and dipyridamole have no role.
Early-morning rest pain with transient ST elevation, no troponin rise and normal coronaries is vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina: treat with CCBs and nitrates.
Inferior STEMI (II, III, aVF) is due to RCA occlusion in ~80%. Check V4R for RV infarction: give fluids and avoid nitrates.
Inferior STEMI with cardiogenic shock: emergency PCI of the culprit artery is the only intervention that improves survival (SHOCK). Nitrates and beta-blockers worsen hypotension.
Transient ST elevation with near-normal coronaries is vasospasm: a CCB (diltiazem/nifedipine) with nitrates and stopping smoking. Non-selective beta-blockers may worsen spasm.
Resting ST–T changes (LVH strain, LBBB, digoxin, WPW, pacing) make exercise ECG uninterpretable; use functional imaging or CT coronary angiography.
Stable NSTEMI already on aspirin, nitrate and LMWH: load a P2Y12 inhibitor to complete DAPT, then angiography within 24 h. Lysis is harmful without ST elevation.
